# Exploring stacking methods for software effort estimation with hyperparameter tuning

Maryam Hassanali [1] [ •] Mohammadreza Soltanaghaei [1] [ •] Taghi Javdani Gandomani [2] [ •] Farsad Zamani Boroujeni [3]

Received: 10 May 2024 / Revised: 29 October 2024 / Accepted: 30 October 2024 / Published online: 25 February 2025
� The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2024

Abstract

This study explores the use of stacking ensemble methods for software effort estimation, leveraging the ISBSG dataset. The
research compares individual machine learning models such as Support Vector Regression (SVR), Random Forest,
AdaBoost, LASSO, and neural networks with stacked models over two phases. In Phase 1, five stacking models were
developed, using SVR, Random Forest, AdaBoost, LASSO, and a neural network as base models. In Phase 2, four stacking
models incorporated two neural networks as base models combined with different metamodels. The results indicate that
stacking models with SVR as the metamodel outperformed individual models and other ensemble methods, especially in
terms of MAE, MSE, MMRE, and MdMRE evaluation metrics. Friedman Test and Nemenyi Post-Hoc Test validated the
results. These findings suggest that using SVR as the metamodel leads to improved accuracy and reliability in effort
estimation, offering significant advantages for project management by enhancing predictive precision and optimizing

resource allocation.

Keywords Software effort estimation � Stacked generalization � Stacked ensemble learning � SVR � Random forest �
AdaBoost


1 Introduction

Project management plays a vital role in software product
development, covering the entire process from beginning to
end. A crucial aspect of project management is software
effort estimation, which significantly influences how a
project is planned and monitored to meet deadlines and
budget constraints. Estimating the effort needed for software projects involves various methods to forecast the total
work required, and it is often seen as one of the most
difficult and intricate tasks that software companies
encounter [1]. The terms ‘‘cost estimation’’ and ‘‘effort

& Mohammadreza Soltanaghaei
soltan@khuisf.ac.ir

estimation’’ in software development are frequently used
interchangeably in software engineering research and project management, as effort is the main factor influencing
cost. In the end, software cost estimation serves as an
indication of the anticipated effort needed to successfully
complete a project [2, 3].
Accurate effort estimation is crucial, yet it comes with
several inherent challenges. One significant issue is the
variability in project conditions, such as differences in
methodologies, team experience, and project scope, which
complicates standardization. Additionally, software projects often undergo changes during development, introducing unpredictability into the estimation process.
Another key challenge is the lack of historical data,
including the knowledge and experience of experts from
previous projects. When this information is missing or
incomplete, it makes the estimation process more difficult,
as accuracy relies heavily on having access to reliable,
comparable data from past projects. Moreover, the nature
of software engineering projects—being human-driven,
non-repetitive, and frequently affected by changes—makes
## 123

241 Page 2 of 20 Cluster Computing (2025) 28:241


it hard to quantify effort. These factors all contribute to the
complexity of estimating software effort [4].
Accurate cost estimation helps project managers prioritize and organize software development efforts in line with
an organization’s overall strategic goals, facilitating
appropriate resource allocation. Effective estimation is
crucial not only for budgeting but also for contract negotiations, tendering, scheduling, and project control.
Underestimation can lead to insufficient budgets and delays
in project completion, resulting in inadequate resource
allocation and, consequently, lower software quality [5].
On the other hand, overestimation can cause a company to
lose out on tenders or over-allocate resources, making
projects less competitive [6].
As outlined in [1, 7], software effort estimation techniques are categorized into algorithmic and non-algorithmic methods. Algorithmic techniques employ
mathematical equations to estimate software effort and
cost, often using metrics like source lines of code (SLOC)
and function points. While algorithmic methods offer
advantages such as consistency and scalability, they can be
difficult to apply and require extensive data on the current
project. Additionally, these techniques can become
unwieldy when dealing with rapidly changing project

environments or limited data.

In contrast, non-algorithmic techniques are simpler to
implement but depend significantly on having complete
and accurate information from previous similar projects.
These methods create estimates by making comparisons
and inferences, usually by examining historical data from
earlier software projects or relevant datasets. Common
non-algorithmic approaches include analogy-based estimation and expert judgment. Analogy-based estimation
involves estimating the costs of a new software project by
comparing it to similar historical projects, using data from
past projects to forecast the necessary effort. The expert
judgment method, on the other hand, relies on the knowledge and experience of professionals who have worked on
similar projects [8]. The effectiveness of this approach
depends on the expert’s knowledge of similar past projects.
Nonetheless, expert judgment may be influenced by personal biases and limited access to complete data, which
makes it especially valuable in situations where gathering
data is challenging [1].
Machine learning-based approaches have attracted
considerable interest in recent years due to their capability
to model complex, non-linear relationships between variables. These methods provide greater flexibility and accuracy, especially in scenarios where traditional nonalgorithmic techniques may not suffice. By recognizing
patterns in historical data, machine learning algorithms can
manage larger datasets and produce more accurate predictions, even when dealing with incomplete or noisy data.
## 123


The popularity of machine learning methods in software
effort estimation has surged because they can extract
valuable insights from data through automated learning
processes. These algorithms excel at modeling complex
problems that are challenging to program explicitly, closely resembling the human learning process. With the
recent advancements in predictive algorithms, machine
learning techniques are now widely utilized in effort estimation [9]. Today, thanks to advancements in predictive
algorithms, machine learning techniques are commonly
used for effort estimation. As the need for quicker and
more precise predictions increases, machine learning
remains essential, especially when traditional methods face
challenges with data quality or have to handle incomplete
information [10].

1.1 Motivation

Accurate software effort estimation is crucial for effective

project management, impacting budget planning, scheduling, and resource allocation. However, traditional estimation methods, whether algorithmic or non-algorithmic,
often face challenges like data noise, variability in project
characteristics, and incomplete historical data. These issues
can result in inaccurate predictions, leading to either underresourced projects or inflated budgets. Driven by the need
for more reliable and adaptive estimation techniques, this
study explores the use of stacking ensemble methods in
machine learning. By combining various models, stacking
has the potential to tackle the unpredictability and data
imperfections typical of software development projects,
with the goal of producing more accurate estimates and
enhancing project planning and resource allocation.

1.2 Research problem

After all traditional estimation methods did not prove so

successful most of the times because either there is not

enough data or significant noise, wide variability in software project characteristics. Additionally, owners of datasets are hesitant to share completely in a preliminary stage
which leads to lack of data making estimates unreliable. A
promising solution is utilizing machine learning-based
approaches, though they are very sensitive to data imperfections and rely on individual algorithms each with the
chance of bias causing lack of prediction performance. As
a way to get around these boundaries, ensemble methods—
including boosting, bagging, and stacking—have been
developed to combine multiple models in efforts to
strengthen overall prediction [11]. This study explores the
use of a two-level stacking ensemble method, aiming to
enhance the accuracy of software effort estimation by
mitigating the effects of data noise and algorithmic bias.

Cluster Computing (2025) 28:241 Page 3 of 20 241


1.3 Research objectives

1. To evaluate the effectiveness of stacking ensemble
methods in improving the accuracy of software effort
estimation by combining multiple machine learning
algorithms and to explore how these improvements can
inform project management practices.
2. To compare the predictive performance of various
stacking models with individual models, focusing on key
evaluation metrics such as Mean Absolute Error (MAE),
Mean Squared Error (MSE), Mean Magnitude of Relative Error (MMRE), Median Magnitude of Relative Error
(MdMRE), Percentage relative error deviation (Pred(x)),
and R [2] score.

3. To identify the most effective combination of base
models and metamodels in the stacking approach for
optimal software effort prediction.

1.4 Novelty and contribution

This study sets itself apart from earlier research by examining a wide variety of stacking models, incorporating a
broad range of machine learning algorithms as both base
models and meta-models. In contrast to previous studies
that typically restrict the number of models or concentrate
on a single meta-model, this research delves into numerous
stacking configurations, featuring multiple neural networks, Support Vector Regression (SVR), Random Forest,
AdaBoost, and LASSO, across two separate phases. These
algorithms were chosen for their complementary abilities
to handle complex and varied data patterns. By merging
these models, the stacked ensemble can leverage the distinct advantages of each algorithm, leading to enhanced
prediction accuracy and robustness. Specifically, this study
highlights the significance of selecting the right metamodel, thoroughly evaluating different algorithms to
identify the most effective meta-model for integrating the
base models—an area that has not been extensively
explored in prior research. Furthermore, considerable
efforts have been dedicated to boosting model accuracy
through careful hyperparameter tuning, utilizing both
RandomizedSearchCV and GridSearchCV methods. While

earlier studies have often overlooked hyperparameter tuning in stacking models, this research illustrates how optimizing these parameters can significantly improve
predictive performance.
This research aims to address the following questions:

Question 1: Do stacking models perform better than
individual models, and how might these improvements
benefit project management practices?


Question 2: Which of the stacking models has a better
prediction based on different evaluation criteria?
Question 3: Using which of the algorithms as a
metamodel leads to a better prediction?

In the continuation of this paper, in Sect. 2, in the
background of the research, the ensemble methods and
machine learning algorithms used in this study are briefly
introduced. Section 3 provides an overview of related
research work estimating software development efforts.
The proposed method has been given in Sect. 4. The results
and discussion are discussed in Sects. 4 and 6 of this study.

2 Research background

Machine learning algorithms are mainly sensitive to noise
in the dataset, which affects the accuracy of prediction

[12]. On the other hand, these algorithms have different
variances and biases in the software effort estimation data.

To overcome the problem of bias, variance, and increase
the model’s accuracy, ensemble machine learning methods
are used in which the output of several algorithms are
combined [12]. There are several ensemble methods,
including bagging, boosting, and stacking.
Stacking differs from boosting and bagging in two ways.
First, a base machine learning algorithm is used in bagging
and boosting methods. Therefore, several identical base
models are trained in different ways, and they are called
homogeneous ensemble techniques. But in the stacking
method, different types of basic algorithms are used, which
are called heterogeneous ensemble techniques. Second, the
stacking method combines the output of base algorithms
using metamodels. At the same time, bagging and boosting
use specific algorithms to combine the output of the base
algorithms. Therefore, developing a stacking model
requires L base models to train the data and a metamodel to

combine the results.

Prediction results are improved when different machine
learning algorithms create the stacking model [13]. The
stacking method combines different algorithms at one or
more levels [13] and aims to reduce bias [14]. This section
provides a brief overview of the machine learning algorithms used in this study, namely LASSO, [1] neural network,
random forest, AdaBoost, and SVR.
Regression algorithms are widely used in machine
learning. Using the standard linear regression method may
lead to overfitting, particularly in the presence of complex
data patterns [15]. LASSO regression uses regularization to
prevent overfitting. LASSO is suitable for problems where

1 Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression.
## 123

241 Page 4 of 20 Cluster Computing (2025) 28:241


the dataset has many features that may be interdependent

[16].
The artificial neural network, or ANN, simulates the
mechanism of the human brain to solve machine learning
problems and is made up of interconnected nodes in different layers. ANN generally consists of an input layer, an
output layer, and a hidden layer, and in deep networks,
neural networks can have more than one hidden layer. In
numerical prediction problems, the neural network’s task is
to learn the optimal weight values assigned to each edge in
the network so that the target variable generates an estimate with minimal residual error [16].
Random forest, one of the bagging methods, is a model
consisting of several trees. The trees that make up a forest
can be shallow or deep. The random forest algorithm is one
of the popular research techniques due to its theoretical
support and known performance in a wide range of problems [17].
AdaBoost is an ensemble boosting method that generates n decision trees during training. When the first decision tree is created, samples incorrectly classified in the
first model have higher priority, and only these samples are
sent to the next model. As a result, higher weights are
assigned to less accurately estimated samples. The model
focuses on the samples with high weight values [16].
The Support Vector Machine (SVM) algorithm can be
applied to both linear and nonlinear classification tasks. In
linear cases, the algorithm searches for a decision surface
that separates two classes of input patterns or vectors. The

distance between this decision surface and the nearest data

points, known as support vectors, is maximized to achieve
optimal separation [18]. For nonlinear data, SVM employs
the kernel trick, which maps the input data into a higherdimensional space, enabling the algorithm to find a nonlinear decision surface.

Support Vector Regression (SVR) extends the principles
of SVM to regression problems, allowing it to model both
linear and nonlinear relationships between input features
and the target variable. The selection of the kernel function
plays a critical role in the performance of SVR, influencing
the model’s ability to capture complex patterns in the data.
This concept has been explored extensively in [19–21].
Ref. [22] examines the systematic mapping of the
ensemble effort estimation methods from 2000 to 2015.

ANN and SVR algorithms are the most widely used base
models in this study’s ensemble methods of estimating
software effort. Reference [23] also examines the systematic mapping of estimation effort prediction using machine
learning methods from 1991 to 2017. ANN and SVR are
also the most widely used algorithms used in this research.
The use of a random forest algorithm has also been
reported. Regression techniques are also mentioned as a
## 123


widely used technique in this research. Therefore, these
algorithms are used here as well.

3 Related works

This section reviews articles that have used stacked

ensemble learning to estimate software development
efforts. Table 1 provides more details about the studies
reviewed in this section. This table presents the year of
publication, the ensemble method and the machine learning
algorithm of each ensemble method, the evaluation measures for measuring the model’s efficiency, and the dataset
used in each of the articles. A summary of the article is also
given in the last column of the table. The stacking method
has been used in all these studies. In some of them, the
stacking method has been compared with other ensemble
methods, and in others, it has been compared with individual algorithms. The most used algorithms in these
studies are different types of regression algorithms, SVR,
neural network, and random forest. Two evaluation criteria,

MAE and MMRE, as well as the ISBSG dataset, are

included in most of these studies.

The table offers a comprehensive overview of existing
research on software effort estimation, particularly
emphasizing ensemble methods such as stacking, bagging,
and boosting. However, a closer examination uncovers
some limitations within these studies. Although ensemble
methods are acknowledged for enhancing prediction
accuracy, many of the cited works overlook the importance
of hyperparameter tuning, which is crucial for optimizing
model performance. Moreover, there is a lack of emphasis
on selecting the metamodel, which significantly impacts
the final predictions. Additionally, prior studies have only
explored and compared a limited number of stacking
models. In contrast, the current research investigates a
wider array of models to determine the best combination,
potentially leading to more accurate and reliable predictions. Addressing these shortcomings would offer a more
comprehensive analysis and better support the methodology employed in this research.

4 Proposed method

Software development projects differ significantly in
methodologies, sizes, and industry contexts, making
accurate estimation a complex task that cannot rely on a
single model. Traditional estimation methods often face
challenges due to data imperfections like noise, outliers,
and limited feature sets, which can lead to less accurate
predictions. Stacking, an effective ensemble learning
technique, helps overcome these issues by leveraging the

strengths of various base models. Each base model presents
distinct benefits to consider. By using a meta-model that
effectively combines these varied predictions, stacking can
minimize both bias and variance, leading to better predictive accuracy. Given how crucial accurate effort estimation
is for successful project planning and resource allocation,
stacking methods offer a flexible and adaptive solution that
can surpass traditional single-model techniques.
In the following section, we will examine the proposed
method in more detail. The various steps of the proposed
method have been summarized in Fig. 1. In this study, a
large number of stacking models have been investigated
compared to previous studies. In the continuation of this
section, the details of the preprocessing stage and the
proposed model have been presented.

4.1 Dataset

ISBSG Dataset [33] gathering a reliable source of many
recent software projects from various industries. Version
## 123


R12019 of this dataset, including 253 features (columns)
and 9178 rows, has been used in this research. Other
datasets, such as the Promise software engineering repository or the COCOMO dataset, are obsolete or unreliable

[9]. The ISBSG dataset contains several features unrelated
to software effort estimation and many missing values,
duplicate data, correlated features, and categorical data.
Therefore, there is a need for preprocessing operations to
convert data into an acceptable format of machine learning
algorithms [12].

4.2 Feature selection

In [34], a systematic mapping study was carried out on 107
research papers, resulting in the identification of 20 of the
most commonly used independent features for estimating
system development effort from the ISBSG dataset. The
researchers implemented a filtering process to focus on the
most frequently utilized variables, ensuring that only those
with a Data Quality Rating of A or B were included to

Cluster Computing (2025) 28:241 Page 7 of 20 241


Fig. 1 The process flow
chart for the proposed stacking
models



guarantee data reliability. This analysis reduced the pool of
71 available variables to 20 essential features, which were
then analyzed for their usage patterns, distribution, and
rates of missing data. Following this, features that showed
high correlation were removed from the machine learning
process to avoid redundancy and enhance model generalization. In the end, the chosen features, detailed in Table 2,
were prepared for further preprocessing. This table also
includes the type of each variable along with a comprehensive description.

4.3 Dataset preprocessing

First, duplicate rows are eliminated from the dataset, 120
duplicate rows are identified, and 9058 remain. Missing
values are eliminated or lost data [35]. Researchers have
extensively studied the impact of missing values on predictions. When data is missing, some information is
inevitably lost, which diminishes the effectiveness of
software effort estimation techniques [36]. Therefore,
managing missing values is essential. One of the techniques for replacing missing values is KNN Imputation.
This technique was chosen because it maintains the relationships between data points by leveraging the similarity


of neighboring values. This makes it more appropriate for
datasets with complex patterns, unlike simpler methods
such as mean or median imputation, which can introduce
bias and oversimplify the data, ultimately distorting predictive models [37].
This technique is a widely recognized and straightforward method that utilizes samples from the surrounding
area to replace missing values, filling in continuous
numerical gaps by averaging the k nearest neighbors [38].
Samples with available features (those without missing
values) that are similar are deemed close. In this study, we
applied the KNN Imputation technique to fill in these
missing values. To determine the best k, we tested a variety
of candidate values (such as 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, and 13) using
fivefold cross-validation. This method divides the dataset
into five equal segments, using four segments for training
and one for validation in each fold. We explored different k
values, implementing KNN imputation and evaluating
performance metrics like mean squared error (MSE) or
mean absolute error (MAE). The k value that yielded the
lowest validation error was chosen as the optimal number
of nearest neighbors, which in this case is k = 11.
The next step is to identify outliers, which are data
points that stand out significantly from other values in the

same group. For this purpose, we used DBSCAN (DensityBased Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise), a
popular density-based clustering algorithm. We chose
DBSCAN for outlier detection because it can identify
clusters of various shapes and handle noise effectively,
enhancing the quality of the data used in predictive models.
By accurately detecting and removing outliers, DBSCAN
minimizes noise that could adversely affect model performance, unlike K-means or hierarchical clustering, which
have difficulty with non-uniform clusters and outliers [39].
DBSCAN is particularly effective in detecting outliers
by measuring the density of points within a given region.
This method relies on two key parameters: epsilon (e),
which defines the radius of the neighborhood around each
data point, and minPts, which specifies the minimum
number of points required to form a dense cluster [39].
## 123


Choosing appropriate values for e and minPts is crucial, as
small values of e may fail to group similar data points,
leading to overly fragmented clusters, while large values
may merge distinct clusters and misidentify noise points.
In this research, minPts was set equal to the number of
features in the dataset, following common best practices for
DBSCAN implementation [40]. To find the optimal value
for epsilon (e), we used the Elbow Method, a common
approach in clustering [40]. We calculated the mean distance between each point and its k-nearest neighbors
(where k = minPts - 1) and plotted these distances in a
k-distance graph, with the x-axis showing sorted points and
the y-axis their distances. The ‘‘elbow’’ of the curve, where
the rate of distance increase slows down, indicated the
optimal e. From the plot, we chose e = 100. This allowed
DBSCAN to identify clusters and detect 135 outliers,

Cluster Computing (2025) 28:241 Page 9 of 20 241


which were then removed to improve data quality and
model performance. The Elbow Method provided a clear
and visual way to select e, helping DBSCAN handle noise
and detect clusters effectively.
In order to facilitate compatibility with various Python
libraries and machine learning algorithms, categorical
features are transformed into numeric representations
through the utilization of the get_dummies method provided by the Pandas library. Since the data attributes span
different ranges, it’s essential to standardize them to ensure
all values are on a comparable scale. To achieve this, the
StandardScaler method is applied. This technique adjusts

the data so that its distribution has a mean of zero and a

standard deviation of one, allowing for consistent comparison across features.
The preprocessing steps taken in this study were
essential for improving the quality of the dataset and
enhancing model performance. By employing KNN
imputation to address missing values, we maintained the
integrity and completeness of the data, allowing models to

learn from a more robust and consistent dataset. Stan
dardizing the data ensured that all features were on the
same scale, which was especially advantageous for algorithms that depend on properly scaled inputs. Additionally,
outlier detection and removal using DBSCAN helped
eliminate noise, enabling the models to concentrate on
significant patterns. These combined preprocessing efforts
led to more accurate, stable, and generalizable models, as
evidenced by improvements in key performance metrics
like MAE and MSE. In summary, the preprocessing steps
were crucial in refining the dataset and optimizing the
performance of the predictive models.

4.4 Proposed model

This paper presents a two-level stacked ensemble method
aimed at improving the accuracy of software effort estimation through the integration of various machine learning
models. In the first level, multiple heterogeneous base
models, each with unique strengths, are trained independently on the same dataset. The predictions generated by
these base models are then used as new input features for
the second level, where a meta-model is introduced. The
meta-model’s purpose is to learn the best way to combine
the predictions from the base models, utilizing their individual outputs. Acting as the final decision-maker, the
meta-model refines the combined predictions. This procedure is depicted in Fig. 2. This study has studied and
compared the stacking models with various machine
learning algorithms as base models and metamodels.
As shown in Table 3, this study predicts the software
effort estimation using ensemble stacking methods in two
phases. The first phase has used four base models in the


first level and one metamodel in the second level. A total of
5 different two-level stacking models are trained and tested
in this phase. Here, SVR, random forest, AdaBoost,
LASSO, and neural network algorithms are used once as
the second level metamodel, and the rest of the algorithms
are used in the first level as base models, details of which
have given in Table 3. Each of these models were chosen
for their complementary strengths in handling complex and
diverse data patterns in software effort estimation:

- SVR: effective in capturing non-linear relationships
between features, making it suitable for datasets with
complex interactions [18].

- Random forest: robust to overfitting and provides
stability, especially when there are noisy data points

[41]. Its ability to handle high-dimensional data makes

it ideal for effort estimation tasks.

- AdaBoost: focuses on improving the accuracy of weak
learners by emphasizing difficult-to-predict instances,
resulting in improved prediction performance [42].

- LASSO: useful for feature selection and regularization,
particularly effective when the dataset contains a large
number of correlated or irrelevant features [43].

- Neural networks: capable of modeling intricate patterns
due to their ability to learn complex, non-linear
representations. Neural networks are especially powerful in dealing with large datasets with diverse features,
as they can capture interactions between variables that
other models may miss [44].

By integrating these various models, the stacked
ensemble can take advantage of their unique strengths to
enhance the overall accuracy and reliability of the predictions. Additionally, neural networks, support vector
regression (SVR), and random forests are some of the most
commonly used and precise machine learning algorithms in
the area of effort estimation [23].
Two different neural networks at the first level are used
as base models in the second phase. A deep neural network
has 8 hidden layers with 1000 neurons in each layer, and
another neural network has a hidden 30,000-neuron layer, a
shallow neural network. A total of 4 stacking models are
examined in the second phase; the details of the base and
metamodel models of each have been given in Table 3.
In this article, we use 5-Fold Cross-Validation to assess
the model’s performance. This technique splits the dataset
into five equal segments, using four segments for training
and one for testing in each iteration. This cycle is repeated
five times, allowing each subset to act as the test set once.
By averaging the outcomes from all folds, 5-Fold CrossValidation offers a strong and dependable estimate of the
model’s performance, while minimizing the risk of overfitting and making the most of the available data.

4.5 Adjusting Model hyperparameter

In this study, we conducted hyperparameter tuning in two
phases, starting with RandomizedSearchCV for initial
exploration and then moving on to GridSearchCV for more
precise optimization. We opted for RandomizedSearchCV
in the first phase because it efficiently searches through a
large hyperparameter space by randomly sampling combinations. This approach is especially useful in high-dimensional settings, where exhaustive methods like
GridSearchCV can be both computationally expensive and
time-consuming. As shown by Bergstra and Bengio [45],
random search is more likely to uncover high-performing
hyperparameter settings by covering a broader area of the
search space without needing to evaluate every single
combination, making it a smart choice for tuning complex
models like those in this stacking ensemble.
## 123


After identifying promising ranges with RandomizedSearchCV, we used GridSearchCV to refine our search
within those areas. This second phase ensured that we
tested all combinations within the selected ranges exhaustively, increasing the chances of finding the optimal
hyperparameters. The combination of these two methods
strikes a balance between exploration and exploitation:
RandomizedSearchCV quickly narrows down the search
space, while GridSearchCV guarantees that the final tuning
is thorough and precise. By utilizing both methods, we
were able to optimize the performance of the stacking
models both efficiently and accurately.

4.6 Evaluation measures

In this study, a comprehensive set of evaluation metrics,
including Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Mean Squared
Error (MSE), Mean Magnitude of Relative Error (MMRE),

Cluster Computing (2025) 28:241 Page 11 of 20 241


Median Magnitude of Relative Error (MdMRE),
Pred(0.25), and R [2] score, were chosen to ensure robust and
multidimensional assessment of model performance in

software effort estimation. These metrics were selected for

their ability to capture different aspects of prediction
accuracy. For example, MAE and MSE provide absolute
and squared error measurements, respectively, giving
insight into the average prediction error and penalizing
larger deviations more heavily. MMRE and MdMRE are
widely used in software estimation studies as they normalize errors relative to the actual values, making them
useful for comparing models across different datasets.
Pred(0.25) measures the percentage of predictions within a
25% relative error, a critical benchmark in effort estimation
literature. Lastly, R [2] score evaluates the goodness of fit of
the model, showing how well the predicted values align
with actual data. Together, these metrics provide a comprehensive and balanced assessment, covering error magnitude, prediction reliability, and model fit, making them
highly relevant to software effort estimation.
Smaller values for MMRE, MdMRE, MSE, MAE, and
larger values for Pred(0.25) indicate better prediction.
MMRE, Pred(0.25), MdMRE, MAE are the most widely
used evaluation measures in estimating software effort

[23]. All of them have been used to evaluate the model in
this study. In addition, R2score has been used to examine

the results. Below is the formula of each of these evalua
tion criteria.

Mean magnitude of Relative error (MMRE): in some
research works, the average difference between the estimated cost of the model and the actual cost for all samples
is used to evaluate the model’s accuracy and can be calculated using the following formula. N represents the
number of projects being evaluated.

5.1 Statistical analysis

To strengthen our conclusions and address the concern of
statistical significance when comparing the individual
models with the stacking models, we conducted several
statistical tests: the Friedman Test and the Nemenyi PostHoc Test. These non-parametric tests are well-suited for
our experiment as they enable comparisons across multiple
models over various datasets or evaluation metrics, without
requiring the assumption of normality in data distribution.

Cluster Computing (2025) 28:241 Page 17 of 20 241

**f** **f** **f** **f** **f** **f** **f** **f**


We applied the Friedman test to identify significant differences in performance among all models, taking into
account the six evaluation metrics used: MAE, MSE,
MMRE, MdMRE, Pred(0.25), and R [2] score. This test was
selected because it is appropriate for comparing multiple
models across metrics when the normality assumptions are
not met, which is the case for software effort estimation

data.

The hypothesis tested was:

- Null hypothesis (H0): there are no significant differences between the individual models and stacking

models.

- Alternative hypothesis (H1): there are significant
differences between the models.

**f** **f** **f** **f** **f** **f** **f** **f**


For this analysis, the test yielded a test statistic of 43.56
with 14 degrees of freedom, reflecting the variance in
performance ranks among the 15 different models evaluated (both individual and stacking configurations). This test
statistic is calculated from the ranks assigned to each
model’s performance for each metric, where a higher test
statistic indicates greater differences in model ranks across
metrics.

To determine if this observed difference was statistically
significant, we compared it to the critical chi-square value
for a significance level of 0.15 (v [2] = 23.685). Since the test
statistic (43.56) exceeds this critical value (23.685), we
rejected the null hypothesis, concluding that significant
differences exist in model performance across the selected
metrics. This result supports that stacking models generally
outperformed individual models, justifying the ensemble
approach used in this study.
Following the significant result of the Friedman test, we
applied the Nemenyi post-hoc test to determine which
specific models differ significantly from each other. The
Nemenyi test compares the performance of pairs of models
based on their average ranks across all metrics, with a
critical difference (CD) value of 7.80, calculated using the
following formula:

**f** **f** **f** **f** **f** **f** **f** **f**


f
**f** i f **f** i f **f** i f **f** i f **f** i f **f** i f **f** i f **f**
k kð þ 1Þ

6n


Plugging these values into the formula gives a critical
difference of 7.80. This means that if the average rank
difference between any two models exceeds 7.80, that
difference is statistically significant.
The Nemenyi test confirms that stacking models, particularly those using SVR as the metamodel, significantly
outperform individual models like Random Forest and
AdaBoost in terms of overall predictive performance.
Thus, the Nemenyi test reinforces the conclusion that SVRbased stacking models yield superior predictive accuracy,
validating the effectiveness of the ensemble approach for

software effort estimation.

6 Conclusion and future work

This paper examines several stacking models to determine
which combination of algorithms used to create these
models has better predictive ability in software effort
estimation. Then, the base models used in building the
stacking models are individually evaluated and compared
with the stacking models. Stacking models have been
investigated in two phases.
In the first phase, 4 base models at the first level and one

metamodel at the second level were used. The results show

that when SVR is used as metamodel and LASSO, random
forest, AdaBoost, and neural network algorithms have been
used as the base models, the best prediction is made
according to MAE, MSE, MMRE, and MdMRE measures.
When AdaBoost is used as the metamodel and LASSO,
random forest, SVR, and neural network algorithms as the
base models, the highest value is obtained in the Pred(0.25)

measure.

In the second phase, two different neural networks were
used as the base model at the first level and a metamodel at
the second level. The results show that when the stacking

model is combined with SVR metamodel and two neural

networks as base models, the best prediction is made
according to MAE, MSE, MMRE, and MdMRE measures.

**f** **f** **f** **f** **f** **f** **f** **f** Also, the ensemble model with AdaBoost metamodel and

two neural networks in the first layer has the highest
Pred(0.25) value. According to the R [2] score measure, all
models studied in two phases have better accuracy than
regression. Therefore, according to this research, and previous research, using the SVR algorithm as a metamodel of
a stacking model can lead to more accurate results based on
most evaluation criteria, and they have also made better
predictions than individual models. These findings are
important for project managers, as they can leverage the
improved predictions to enhance resource allocation,
manage project timelines more effectively, and reduce

risks.

- q a is the critical value from the studentized range

Statistical analysis through the Friedman Test and
Nemenyi Post-Hoc Test shows that stacking models,
especially those utilizing SVR as the metamodel, significantly surpass individual models in terms of MAE, MSE,
MMRE, and MdMRE. This evidence strongly supports the
idea that stacking models provide better prediction performance for software effort estimation, offering

notable advancements over traditional models.

Given the numerous hyperparameters associated with
ensemble models, particularly in multi-level stacking,
future research could delve into hyperparameter optimization techniques. Approaches like Bayesian optimization or genetic algorithms might be explored to fine-tune
model parameters efficiently. Properly adjusting hyperparameters is essential for ensuring the robustness and
accuracy of ensemble methods, and optimizing these can
greatly enhance prediction outcomes. Future studies could
also examine the computational aspects of stacking models,
such as training and inference times, to assess their scalability for larger datasets or real-time applications. Additionally, strategies like model optimization, parallel
processing, or minimizing the number of base models
could be investigated to boost computational efficiency
without sacrificing prediction accuracy. While this study
concentrated on software effort estimation, there is considerable potential for applying stacking models to other
vital areas in software engineering, such as software fault
prediction. Accurate software fault prediction is crucial for
enhancing software quality by identifying fault-prone
modules early in the development cycle, which leads to
more effective testing and debugging efforts.

Javdani Gandomani controlled the analytical methods and evaluation
of the results. Dr. Farsad Zamani Boroujeni helped Maryam Hassanali
write the manuscript and correct its errors. All authors discussed the
results and contributed to the final manuscript and the preparation of
the revised version of the manuscript.

for the submitted work.
